title: Kashmir Shaivism opening (the Shiva Sutras)
hook: the second thread of the Shiva Sutras says knowledge is bondage, and means the small, limited kind

segments.voice: Yesterday was Kashmir Shaivism opening: a rock that turned over, and the first thread of the Shiva Sutras, consciousness is the self. When a mood took over, did you catch the one noticing it? Day one thousand one hundred forty.

Knowledge is bondage. That's the whole second line of the Shiva Sutras, two words in Sanskrit, jnanam bandhah. Read it cold and it sounds like an attack on school, on books, on curiosity, on everything a library stands for. It isn't. But it's meant to stop you, the way a sign on a door saying do not enter makes you look twice at the door. Yesterday the first thread said consciousness is the self. Today's thread says what goes wrong. Back to the opening of Kashmir Shaivism.
screen: `KNOWLEDGE IS BONDAGE.` → `NOT AN ATTACK ON BOOKS.` → `WHAT GOES WRONG.`

segments.voice: Start with the first thread again. Consciousness is the self, and in this tradition that consciousness is Shiva's own: wide, free, whole. So if that's what we are, why can life feel so cramped? The second thread answers: knowing binds. Commentators in the tradition read the word knowledge here as a particular kind of knowing: limited knowing. The quiet, constant sense of I am only this. Only this body. Only this anxious person with this bank balance and this argument from last week. Not wrong information, but too small a picture of who's doing the knowing. That small picture is the knot. It isn't a punishment, and it isn't a sin in this teaching. It's closer to a habit of seeing. You look at a vast sky through a keyhole long enough, and you start to think the sky is keyhole-shaped. The commentators also notice something gentler underneath. If bondage is a kind of knowing, then freedom is also a kind of knowing. Not a new fact. A recognition. The same consciousness, seeing itself without the keyhole. One school in Kashmir takes its name from this idea, pratyabhijna, recognition: nothing has to be built from scratch, only seen again. On an ordinary day, the small knowing sounds like I'm just not a patient person, or I'm the one who always messes up. Labels that started as information and became walls. The second thread doesn't ask you to stop knowing things. It asks who you think is doing the knowing.
screen: `JNANAM BANDHAH: KNOWING BINDS.` · `LIMITED KNOWING: I AM ONLY THIS.` · `A SKY SEEN THROUGH A KEYHOLE.` · `FREEDOM AS RECOGNITION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: catch one label and widen it. Sit, and let the breath settle. Let a sentence come up that starts with I'm just or I'm only or I always: something you say about yourself. Hold it gently. Then on each out-breath, let the space around it get wider, the way your view grows when you step back from a keyhole and open the door. The label can stay. It just isn't the whole room anymore. If you pray, you can rest in the first thread, consciousness is the self. The bell holds the time.
Kashmir Shaivism opening. The second thread of the Shiva Sutras: jnanam bandhah, knowledge is bondage, the small knowing that says I am only this.
Your line: Kashmir Shaivism opening, the Shiva Sutras. Today, when you hear yourself say I'm just or I always, add three words: and much more. Day one thousand one hundred forty.

howItsDone: Students of Kashmir Shaivism read the Shiva Sutras slowly with a commentary, and the tradition's teachers describe freedom as recognition (pratyabhijna) of one's own nature as Shiva.

fork.setup: you read a sacred line: knowledge is bondage. what do you do with it?
options: ask what kind of knowing binds.
decide the line must be a mistake.
fork.reveal: the commentators ask exactly that: the knowing that binds is the limited sense of I am only this.

original.note: Sanskrit: Shiva Sutra 1.2, knowledge (jnanam) is bondage (bandhah).

what it means: the knowing that binds is the small sense of self, and freedom is recognizing more.

notes: Second of three. Commentary on 1.2 paraphrased in general terms: Kshemaraja reads jnana here as limited or differentiated knowledge (linked to anava mala, the impurity of smallness). Keeper may want the commentary's two readings named more precisely.

'This tradition is sometimes called a path of recognition': pratyabhijna is the name of a school within Kashmir Shaivism (Utpaladeva, Abhinavagupta), not strictly the Shiva Sutras; confirm the phrasing is fair.
Keyhole image is the script's own, not the commentary's.
Sanskrit for 1.2 given as ज्ञानं बन्धः. Confirm.
